chapter: Recent years and early piano influences
title: Earl Hines's unorthodox style
summary: Hines played tenths, without pedal, with percussive intensity; Ramirez lacked his hands.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: But Earl Hines came over and made this record, and his style was so unorthodox; you know, you had to really have the hands in order to play it.
Earl's hands were not that bag.

Oh my goodness! Yeah, he played tenths. And one other thing that made him distinctive, he played without the pedal a lot. And that gave a percussive sound to the piano and intensity, quite a... You know, it wasn't a legato thing; nothing legato...using the pedal was instrumental... Like Fats Waller at that time, because he used to sustain his left hand, J.P., those stride pianists. Earl didn't

need that, because he used to abbreviate his left-hand rhythmic patterns, you know, and then he would lash(?) it with his thumb. He had a... Ooh, he would cut... I saw him break a B-flat once with this thumb, you know...
A string. His touch was very incisive. But it wasn't...
He had a strong touch. It was firm! It was very firm.
But it wasn't heavy, was it.
It was very firm. And he could be delicate when he wanted to be. All without the aid of the pedal. He very seldom used it... To me it didn't sound like he used the pedal at all -- hardly ever.
In the early days. Later on...

In the early days, yeah. Because I think the way he played, he braced his feet; really, that's where he got his power. He used to brace his feet and then look at the audience a lot of times. He was very flashy, you know.

He used to be one of your favorite pianists, I remember! He was one of my favorites, but the thing is, I just didn't have the hands and the power that he had. I had to just... I lost a race... I was impressed with him because he... Actually, I came up with a band, you know.
